items.title: Roger Kellaway interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999
items.q: I’ve only met a handful of players in my whole life that could do it. And I’m not sure that Coltrane is one of them.

ctx.x: Yeah they started listening to him right there.

Yeah. And I happened to walk out on that concert, because I was bored. And it’s extremely difficult to play a solo for 10 or 15 minutes and have it be interesting, and I’ve only met a handful of players in my whole life that could do it. And I’m not sure that Coltrane is one of them. But thinking about my background and having grown up through Dixieland, let’s not just take Dixieland, let’s go back to Stravinsky’s “Serenade in A” for piano. It was written for 78s. In recording, there couldn’t be a movement that…

Yeah, that’s a good statement, and it’s interesting when you think about how music reproduction technology has helped to shape the music. The limits that were put on it, as you say, really affected the way a person could write, and in some cases very positively. I have three minutes to make a statement here.
